description: A large fridge egg needs 10 minutes 10 seconds for a hard-boiled egg with a fully set yolk. Times by size, start, and altitude, from the Williams formula.

examples.result: One extra-large fridge egg, hard-boiled: 10 minutes 55 seconds.
steps: The egg starts at fridge temperature, 4°C, and the water boils at 100°C at sea level.
The hard target is 84°C at the edge of the yolk.
The formula gives 657 seconds, about 10 minutes 55 seconds.
examples.title: One extra-large fridge egg, hard-boiled

examples.result: One medium room-temperature egg, hard-boiled: 8 minutes 10 seconds.
steps: The egg starts at room temperature, 20°C, and the water boils at 100°C.
The formula gives 490 seconds, about 8 minutes 10 seconds.
examples.title: One medium room-temperature egg, hard-boiled

faqs.answer: The grey-green layer is iron sulfide, formed where iron in the yolk meets sulfur from the white after long hot cooking. Stop on time, 10 minutes 10 seconds for a large fridge egg, and move the eggs straight to ice water. Food Network Kitchen found the ring appears by 15 minutes.
faqs.question: Why did my hard-boiled yolk turn green?

faqs.answer: Hard-cooked eggs keep up to 7 days in the refrigerator, in the shell, per USDA guidance. Refrigerate them within 2 hours of cooking. Peeled eggs should be eaten sooner: the USDA expert quoted by Food Network gives peeled eggs 48 hours.
faqs.question: How long do hard-boiled eggs keep?

faqs.answer: Thermal shock. A fridge-cold egg dropped into boiling water warms unevenly and the air pocket at the wide end expands fast. Lower eggs in gently on a spoon, use room-temperature eggs, or prick the wide end with a pin to let the air out.
faqs.question: Why did my hard-boiled eggs crack?

faqs.answer: Yes, for these times. The formula describes an egg lowered into water that is already boiling. Starting in cold water is a different method with its own timing, covered on the cold-start page.
faqs.question: Do I need to boil the water first?

faqs.answer: Trust the timer for your egg size, or sacrifice one egg and cut it open. The ice bath stops the cooking, so a test egg tells you the truth about the batch. If the center is still wet, give the rest one more minute.
faqs.question: How do I know the yolk is set without cutting one open?

felicityNote: Hard-boiled eggs are the week's workhorse: salads, lunchboxes, deviled eggs. Ten minutes, ice water, done.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 84°C for hard-boiled, where ovalbumin denatures.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For a large fridge egg at sea level, hard-boiled: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 100) / (84 - 100)) = 608 seconds, about 10 minutes 10 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Boil the water first
howToSteps.text: Fill a saucepan with enough water to cover the eggs by an inch and bring it to a full rolling boil.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer the moment the first egg touches the water. Keep the water at a gentle boil.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: Boil a large fridge egg for 10 minutes 10 seconds. A medium egg needs 9 minutes 15 seconds, an extra-large 10 minutes 55 seconds, and a jumbo 11 minutes 45 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Ice bath
howToSteps.text: Move the eggs straight to ice water for 10 minutes. This stops the cooking, prevents the green ring, and makes peeling easier.

howToSteps.name: Peel
howToSteps.text: Tap both ends on the counter, roll the egg gently to crack the shell all over, and peel under cold running water.

lede: A large egg straight from the fridge takes 10 minutes 10 seconds in boiling water for a hard-boiled egg: white firm, yolk fully set and pale yellow, no green ring. The yolk edge reaches 84°C, where the white's main protein finishes setting.

title: How Long to Boil Hard-Boiled Eggs
tutorial: A hard-boiled egg is set all the way through: firm white, yolk pale yellow and sliceable, no wet center and no green ring. The formula times the yolk edge reaching 84°C, the temperature where ovalbumin, the main protein of the white, denatures. For a large fridge egg that takes 10 minutes 10 seconds, inside the 10 to 12 minutes that published guides give for a large egg.

The green ring is the thing to avoid, and it comes from heat plus time. When the yolk stays hot for too long, sulfur from the white reacts with iron in the yolk and leaves a grey-green layer. Stopping at 10 minutes 10 seconds and moving the eggs straight into ice water keeps the yolk short of the long hot soak that causes it. Food Network Kitchen found the ring appears by 15 minutes, so there is no need to push past 12.

Size matters most at this doneness, because the extra minutes add up. A medium egg needs 9 minutes 15 seconds, an extra-large 10 minutes 55 seconds, and a jumbo 11 minutes 45 seconds. A room-temperature large egg needs 8 minutes 55 seconds, more than a minute less than from the fridge. Set the timer for the size in your pot, not the size in the recipe.

Altitude stretches hard-boiled times more than any other doneness, because the 84°C target sits close to the lower boiling point. At 5,000 feet the water boils at 94.9°C and a large fridge egg needs 12 minutes 20 seconds. At 7,000 feet it needs 13 minutes 30 seconds. Williams himself noted the formula under-predicts at altitude, so on a mountain, give the eggs a little extra time and check one before you cool the batch.

Peeling is easier with eggs that are a week or so old, because the air cell has grown and the membrane pulls away cleanly. Very fresh eggs stick. An ice bath of 10 minutes helps too: it stops the cooking and shrinks the egg slightly inside the shell.
